screens.title: User and Group Management & System Info
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll ground you in the small set of concepts and commands that control who can do what on a RHEL system. You'll learn why numerical identifiers called UIDs and GIDs matter, how users map to primary and supplementary groups, and where the system keeps account and password data. I'll also show the quick commands used to check a machine’s identity, kernel, disk, memory, and network state. These are the basic checks you will run when auditing a server or troubleshooting a login problem. For example, adding a developer to a shared 'developers' group immediately grants access to group-owned resources without changing individual file permissions. A common source of error is forgetting the append flag when adding groups, which removes previous group memberships; we'll demonstrate that exact pitfall and how to avoid it. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to create users and groups, verify entries in /etc/passwd and /etc/group, lock and unlock accounts safely, and run a short checklist of system information commands to understand system health. Ready to start? Notice the three key topics below: users, groups, and system information — these are the practical tools you'll use daily.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › User & Group Management
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Users, Groups, and Quick System Checks

Understand identifiers, core files, and the commands you’ll use for daily administration.

Duration target: 15 minutes
User Identity
UIDs map users to ownership; UIDs 0-999 are system accounts, regular users start at 1000.
Group Access
Groups bundle permissions. Supplementary groups expand access without changing file owners.
System Info
A few commands reveal hostname, kernel, disk, memory, and network state for troubleshooting.
Explore Key Topics
Create & Manage Users
useradd, passwd, usermod, userdel
Groups & Membership
groupadd, groupmod, groupdel, usermod -aG
System Checks
id, hostnamectl, uname, df -h, free -h, ip a
Visual Concept
Identifiers
Usernames map to UIDs; groups map to GIDs. Files store the name but the kernel uses the numeric IDs.
Core files
/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/group hold the canonical account and group info used by authentication and tools.
Daily commands
A handful of commands let you create and verify accounts and inspect system status quickly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these exercises you will be able to manage user and group identities confidently and collect essential system information. First, you'll understand UIDs and GIDs — the numerical identifiers the kernel uses — and why regular user IDs start at higher numbers to avoid system account collisions. Second, you'll create, modify, and remove user accounts and groups using the standard RHEL commands, and you'll set and rotate passwords. Third, you'll inspect the authoritative system files that store account and group information and use that insight when troubleshooting login or permission issues. Fourth, you'll run quick system checks for hostname, kernel release, disk usage, memory use, and network interface addresses to verify system health. These skills matter because identity and access control are the foundation of system security, and the ability to read the system state quickly helps you triage incidents and report accurate diagnostics. We'll practice a safe lab workflow with clear commands and verification steps so you can reproduce them on your own systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: We will practice these skills with a safe, repeatable sequence: create a group, add a user with a home directory, set a password, verify entries, and then clean up. Always work as root for account creation, and pause before using destructive flags like userdel -r. A concrete scenario: create a 'developers' group, make 'devuser1' a member, verify with id and grep, then lock and unlock the account to test access control. This sequence demonstrates how group membership affects file access and how the shadow file controls login. You'll also run commands to inspect hostname, kernel, disk, memory, and network to form an operational snapshot. Common mistakes to watch for include forgetting the -a flag when adding groups, which replaces supplementary groups instead of appending, and using userdel without checking owned files. We will explicitly show those pitfalls and the verification steps that catch them so you can avoid them in production.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Learning Objectives — Practice

Practice & Safety

A reproducible lab: create group, create user, add to group, set password, verify, lock/unlock, check system info, clean up.

Create group: groupadd developers
Create user: useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash devuser1
Set password: passwd devuser1
Common Mistake
Using usermod -G without -a will remove existing supplementary groups.
Pro tip
Verify changes with id username and grep on the core files before proceeding.

screens.title: UIDs and GIDs: what they are and why they matter
screens.narratorSegment: A User ID, or UID, and a Group ID, or GID, are the precise numerical identifiers the kernel uses to record file ownership and process identity. Humans see usernames and group names, but the kernel maps these to numbers when enforcing permissions. Regular user UIDs typically start at 1000 so they don't collide with system and service accounts that occupy lower numbers. The root account has UID 0 and full privileges. One concrete example: when a file is owned by user alice with UID 1001 and group staff with GID 50, the kernel checks the effective UID and GIDs of the requesting process against those numbers to decide read, write, or execute access. A frequent misconception is to rely on names only — if a user is renamed but the UID remains the same, ownership does not change; tools reference the numeric identifier. Another pitfall is creating users with a low UID that accidentally overlaps system accounts. Key takeaway: manage names for humans, UIDs and GIDs for the system. When you audit permissions, always inspect numeric IDs if behavior seems inconsistent. How might a renamed account still own files? Think about the UID remaining unchanged.

keyIdea.text: UIDs and GIDs are numeric handles the kernel uses to enforce ownership and permissions; names are human-friendly labels mapped to these IDs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › UIDs & GIDs
Definition

Numeric identifiers

UIDs and GIDs are used internally to attribute processes and files to identities. Usernames are mapped to UIDs in /etc/passwd and groups to GIDs in /etc/group.

Concrete example
File owned by alice (UID 1001), group staff (GID 50). The kernel checks numbers, not names, to grant access.
Common misconception
Renaming a user does not change their UID. Files owned by that numeric UID remain owned even if the name changes.
Key Takeaway

Inspect numeric IDs when debugging ownership; keep system and regular UIDs separated.

Analogy

UID = Social Security number

A username is like a person's display name. The UID is the immutable numeric identifier the system trusts for ownership.

Quick check
# show id and numeric mapping
id alice
# shows uid=1001(uid=1001) gid=50(staff) groups=50(staff),100(devs)

screens.title: Creating and verifying a user
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a user is a common, repeatable process: make the account, set a password, and confirm the entries in the system files. Start as root and run useradd with -m to create a home directory and -s to set a default shell. For example, useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash devuser1 creates devuser1, creates a home directory, and places the account in the developers supplementary group. Immediately set a password with passwd devuser1. To verify, use id devuser1 to see the numeric UID, primary GID, and supplementary groups. Also grep devuser1 in /etc/passwd to confirm the home directory and shell fields. This verification is essential because useradd may fail silently if the group doesn't exist or if there are naming conflicts. A common mistake is assuming a successful command created a home directory — always check /home/username and /etc/passwd. Key takeaway: create, secure (password), and verify. How will you confirm the account has the correct shell and group? Creating and verifying a user means use useradd -m to create a home, passwd to set passwords, id and grep to confirm uid, gid, home, and shell.. In practical terms, useradd, passwd, id, and grep for verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Create & Verify User
Step-by-step

Create, set password, verify

Create group first
groupadd developers — ensure supplementary group exists before using -G.
Create user
useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash devuser1
Set password
passwd devuser1 — root can set others' passwords.
Key Takeaway

Always verify with id and grep to confirm UID, GID, home directory, and shell.

Terminal Demo (visual)
# create a group
$ groupadd developers
# create user with home and supplement group
$ useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash devuser1
# set the password
$ passwd devuser1
# verify
$ id devuser1
uid=1001(devuser1) gid=1001(devuser1) groups=1001(devuser1),101(developers)
$ grep '^devuser1:' /etc/passwd
devuser1:x:1001:1001::/home/devuser1:/bin/bash
Check the home path and the shell field in /etc/passwd to confirm defaults.

screens.title: Adding a user to supplementary groups safely
screens.narratorSegment: Supplementary groups extend a user's access without changing their primary group. The correct command pattern is usermod -aG groupname username; the -a stands for append and preserves existing supplementary groups while -G sets a new supplementary group list. A common and damaging mistake is running usermod -G groupname username without -a, which replaces the user's supplementary groups and can inadvertently remove access to resources. Concrete example: if tester1 is already in groups developers and testers and you run usermod -G monitoring tester1, tester1 will lose developers and testers membership and only be in monitoring. To verify after a change, run id tester1 and grep tester1 /etc/group to see membership. If you see unexpected removals, re-add groups explicitly with usermod -aG. Key takeaway: always use -a when adding groups and verify immediately. What verification step will you use in your workflow to catch accidental removals? Adding a user to supplementary groups safely means usermod -ag appends supplementary groups; using -g alone replaces them. always verify group membership after changes.. In practical terms, why -ag matters and how to avoid removing existing group memberships. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Append vs replace
keyIdea.text: usermod -aG appends supplementary groups; using -G alone replaces them. Always verify group membership after changes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Supplementary Groups
Why it matters

Append, don't replace

Supplementary groups give shared access. Use -a to avoid removing previous memberships accidentally.

Correct command
usermod -aG developers tester1 — adds developers without removing others.
Danger
usermod -G monitoring tester1 replaces the full supplementary list and can remove access unexpectedly.
Check your work

Verify with id and /etc/group immediately after changes.

Terminal pattern
# add tester1 to developers safely
$ usermod -aG developers tester1
# verify membership
$ id tester1
uid=1002(tester1) gid=1002(tester1) groups=1002(tester1),101(developers),102(testers)
# inspect /etc/group
$ grep '^developers:' /etc/group
developers:x:101:devuser1,tester1
If membership is missing, re-run usermod with -aG for each group or use a scripted reconciliation.

screens.title: Core account files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group
screens.narratorSegment: Three text files are the canonical sources of user and group data on RHEL: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/group. /etc/passwd stores account fields: username, placeholder for password, UID, GID, GECOS, home directory, and default shell. Historically it also contained password hashes, but modern systems replace the password column with an 'x' because hashed secrets live in /etc/shadow. /etc/shadow contains encrypted password hashes and aging policies and is readable only by root — this separation protects passwords from ordinary users. /etc/group lists group names, their GIDs, and a comma-separated list of supplementary members. When troubleshooting a login or permission error, check /etc/passwd to confirm the user's home and shell, /etc/shadow to see whether the account is locked or password expired, and /etc/group to verify membership. A common misconception is that changing a name in /etc/passwd changes ownership of files — it does not unless the numeric UID is modified. Always examine the numeric IDs when outcomes differ from expectations. Core account files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group means /etc/passwd: account metadata; /etc/shadow: secure password data; /etc/group: group definitions and member lists.. In practical terms, what each file stores and who can read it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Core Account Files

What each file contains

/etc/passwd
Fields: username:x:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell. The 'x' points to /etc/shadow for the password hash.
/etc/shadow
Contains hashed passwords and aging rules. Root-only readability protects passwords from ordinary users.
/etc/group
Groupname:x:GID:member1,member2 — supplementary members listed explicitly here.
When debugging logins, check /etc/passwd for shell or home misconfiguration, and /etc/shadow for locked accounts or expired passwords.
Visual sample
# /etc/passwd example
devuser1:x:1001:1001:Dev User:/home/devuser1:/bin/bash
# /etc/group example
developers:x:101:devuser1,tester1
# /etc/shadow (root-only) shows hashed passwords and aging
Misconception

Editing the username in /etc/passwd without adjusting the UID will not change file ownership; ownership is numeric.

screens.title: Locking and unlocking accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Locking and unlocking accounts is a controlled way to prevent login without deleting the account. The commands usermod -L username and usermod -U username toggle lock state by modifying the password field in /etc/shadow or setting a lock flag depending on system tooling. A practical scenario: temporarily disabling devuser1 during maintenance prevents interactive login while preserving home and files. After locking, attempting su - devuser1 should fail with an authentication error; unlocking restores access. A common misconception is that locking removes the user’s files — it doesn’t. Another is confusing disabling a shell versus locking the account; changing the shell to /sbin/nologin prevents shell access but does not change password state. To verify a lock, inspect /etc/shadow root-only or attempt authentication and check the error. Key takeaway: locks are reversible and safe for temporary suspension. Consider which method suits your aim: lock the account or change the shell for service accounts. Locking and unlocking accounts means use usermod -l to lock and -u to unlock accounts; this blocks login but preserves data and identity.. In practical terms, usermod -l and usermod -u to control login access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Temporary suspension
keyIdea.text: Use usermod -L to lock and -U to unlock accounts; this blocks login but preserves data and identity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Lock / Unlock
Commands

Lock and unlock

# lock an account
usermod -L devuser1
# attempt login should fail
$ su - devuser1
Authentication failure
# unlock
usermod -U devuser1
Locking is reversible and preserves home directories and file ownership. Use for maintenance or investigations.
Comparison

Lock vs change shell

Changing a shell to /sbin/nologin stops interactive shells but does not change password state. Locking manipulates the shadow password and prevents all password-based authentication for the account.
Pro tip

Use locking for temporary suspension; change shell for long-term service accounts where you want no interactive login.

screens.title: Group management: create, rename, delete
screens.narratorSegment: Groups let you manage sets of users and simplify permission management. Use groupadd groupname to create a new group. To rename a group use groupmod -n newname oldname, which updates the name while preserving the GID. Deleting a group with groupdel groupname removes the group entry, but groupdel will fail if users are still members or if the group is a primary group for an existing user. Safely delete groups by first removing users from supplementary membership or reassigning primary groups. A scenario: you create developers, add users, then decide to rename to devs; run groupmod -n devs developers, then verify /etc/group and file ownership. A misconception is assuming groupdel cleans up files owned by the group's GID; it does not. Files retain their numeric GID and may become associated with an unlisted GID. Key takeaway: plan group deletions, reassign or remove memberships first, and verify with grep in /etc/group. Group management: create, rename, delete means create with groupadd, rename with groupmod -n, delete only after ensuring no users rely on the group.. In practical terms, groupadd, groupmod, groupdel and safe deletion practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Quick system information commands
screens.narratorSegment: When you join a troubleshooting session, a short set of commands gives you the machine's identity and resource snapshot. Use hostname to show the configured host name; hostnamectl provides richer details including operating system and architecture. Use uname -r to show kernel release and uname -a for the full kernel and platform details. For storage, df -h reports mounted file system usage with human-readable sizes; this helps quickly spot a nearly full root partition. For memory, free -h shows total, used, and free physical and swap memory in human-friendly units. For network, ip a lists interfaces and their addresses; it replaces the deprecated ifconfig. A concrete example: if a service fails to start, check df -h to ensure the disk is not full, then check free -h for memory pressure, and ip a to verify the service’s binding address exists. A misconception is assuming disk space and memory are unrelated; both can contribute to service outages. Key takeaway: run this short checklist to gather context before deep troubleshooting. 2: enp0s3: inet 192.0.2.10/24

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll ground you in the small set of concepts and commands that control who can do what on a RHEL system. You'll learn why numerical identifiers called UIDs and GIDs matter, how users map to primary and supplementary groups, and where the system keeps account and password data. I'll also show the quick commands used to check a machine’s identity, kernel, disk, memory, and network state. These are the basic checks you will run when auditing a server or troubleshooting a login problem. For example, adding a developer to a shared 'developers' group immediately grants access to group-owned resources without changing individual file permissions. A common source of error is forgetting the append flag when adding groups, which removes previous group memberships; we'll demonstrate that exact pitfall and how to avoid it. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to create users and groups, verify entries in /etc/passwd and /etc/group, lock and unlock accounts safely, and run a short checklist of system information commands to understand system health. Ready to start? Notice the three key topics below: users, groups, and system information — these are the practical tools you'll use daily.

By the end of these exercises you will be able to manage user and group identities confidently and collect essential system information. First, you'll understand UIDs and GIDs — the numerical identifiers the kernel uses — and why regular user IDs start at higher numbers to avoid system account collisions. Second, you'll create, modify, and remove user accounts and groups using the standard RHEL commands, and you'll set and rotate passwords. Third, you'll inspect the authoritative system files that store account and group information and use that insight when troubleshooting login or permission issues. Fourth, you'll run quick system checks for hostname, kernel release, disk usage, memory use, and network interface addresses to verify system health. These skills matter because identity and access control are the foundation of system security, and the ability to read the system state quickly helps you triage incidents and report accurate diagnostics. We'll practice a safe lab workflow with clear commands and verification steps so you can reproduce them on your own systems.

We will practice these skills with a safe, repeatable sequence: create a group, add a user with a home directory, set a password, verify entries, and then clean up. Always work as root for account creation, and pause before using destructive flags like userdel -r. A concrete scenario: create a 'developers' group, make 'devuser1' a member, verify with id and grep, then lock and unlock the account to test access control. This sequence demonstrates how group membership affects file access and how the shadow file controls login. You'll also run commands to inspect hostname, kernel, disk, memory, and network to form an operational snapshot. Common mistakes to watch for include forgetting the -a flag when adding groups, which replaces supplementary groups instead of appending, and using userdel without checking owned files. We will explicitly show those pitfalls and the verification steps that catch them so you can avoid them in production.

A User ID, or UID, and a Group ID, or GID, are the precise numerical identifiers the kernel uses to record file ownership and process identity. Humans see usernames and group names, but the kernel maps these to numbers when enforcing permissions. Regular user UIDs typically start at 1000 so they don't collide with system and service accounts that occupy lower numbers. The root account has UID 0 and full privileges. One concrete example: when a file is owned by user alice with UID 1001 and group staff with GID 50, the kernel checks the effective UID and GIDs of the requesting process against those numbers to decide read, write, or execute access. A frequent misconception is to rely on names only — if a user is renamed but the UID remains the same, ownership does not change; tools reference the numeric identifier. Another pitfall is creating users with a low UID that accidentally overlaps system accounts. Key takeaway: manage names for humans, UIDs and GIDs for the system. When you audit permissions, always inspect numeric IDs if behavior seems inconsistent. How might a renamed account still own files? Think about the UID remaining unchanged.

Creating a user is a common, repeatable process: make the account, set a password, and confirm the entries in the system files. Start as root and run useradd with -m to create a home directory and -s to set a default shell. For example, useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash devuser1 creates devuser1, creates a home directory, and places the account in the developers supplementary group. Immediately set a password with passwd devuser1. To verify, use id devuser1 to see the numeric UID, primary GID, and supplementary groups. Also grep devuser1 in /etc/passwd to confirm the home directory and shell fields. This verification is essential because useradd may fail silently if the group doesn't exist or if there are naming conflicts. A common mistake is assuming a successful command created a home directory — always check /home/username and /etc/passwd. Key takeaway: create, secure (password), and verify. How will you confirm the account has the correct shell and group? Creating and verifying a user means use useradd -m to create a home, passwd to set passwords, id and grep to confirm uid, gid, home, and shell.. In practical terms, useradd, passwd, id, and grep for verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Supplementary groups extend a user's access without changing their primary group. The correct command pattern is usermod -aG groupname username; the -a stands for append and preserves existing supplementary groups while -G sets a new supplementary group list. A common and damaging mistake is running usermod -G groupname username without -a, which replaces the user's supplementary groups and can inadvertently remove access to resources. Concrete example: if tester1 is already in groups developers and testers and you run usermod -G monitoring tester1, tester1 will lose developers and testers membership and only be in monitoring. To verify after a change, run id tester1 and grep tester1 /etc/group to see membership. If you see unexpected removals, re-add groups explicitly with usermod -aG. Key takeaway: always use -a when adding groups and verify immediately. What verification step will you use in your workflow to catch accidental removals? Adding a user to supplementary groups safely means usermod -ag appends supplementary groups; using -g alone replaces them. always verify group membership after changes.. In practical terms, why -ag matters and how to avoid removing existing group memberships. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Three text files are the canonical sources of user and group data on RHEL: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/group. /etc/passwd stores account fields: username, placeholder for password, UID, GID, GECOS, home directory, and default shell. Historically it also contained password hashes, but modern systems replace the password column with an 'x' because hashed secrets live in /etc/shadow. /etc/shadow contains encrypted password hashes and aging policies and is readable only by root — this separation protects passwords from ordinary users. /etc/group lists group names, their GIDs, and a comma-separated list of supplementary members. When troubleshooting a login or permission error, check /etc/passwd to confirm the user's home and shell, /etc/shadow to see whether the account is locked or password expired, and /etc/group to verify membership. A common misconception is that changing a name in /etc/passwd changes ownership of files — it does not unless the numeric UID is modified. Always examine the numeric IDs when outcomes differ from expectations. Core account files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group means /etc/passwd: account metadata; /etc/shadow: secure password data; /etc/group: group definitions and member lists.. In practical terms, what each file stores and who can read it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Locking and unlocking accounts is a controlled way to prevent login without deleting the account. The commands usermod -L username and usermod -U username toggle lock state by modifying the password field in /etc/shadow or setting a lock flag depending on system tooling. A practical scenario: temporarily disabling devuser1 during maintenance prevents interactive login while preserving home and files. After locking, attempting su - devuser1 should fail with an authentication error; unlocking restores access. A common misconception is that locking removes the user’s files — it doesn’t. Another is confusing disabling a shell versus locking the account; changing the shell to /sbin/nologin prevents shell access but does not change password state. To verify a lock, inspect /etc/shadow root-only or attempt authentication and check the error. Key takeaway: locks are reversible and safe for temporary suspension. Consider which method suits your aim: lock the account or change the shell for service accounts. Locking and unlocking accounts means use usermod -l to lock and -u to unlock accounts; this blocks login but preserves data and identity.. In practical terms, usermod -l and usermod -u to control login access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Groups let you manage sets of users and simplify permission management. Use groupadd groupname to create a new group. To rename a group use groupmod -n newname oldname, which updates the name while preserving the GID. Deleting a group with groupdel groupname removes the group entry, but groupdel will fail if users are still members or if the group is a primary group for an existing user. Safely delete groups by first removing users from supplementary membership or reassigning primary groups. A scenario: you create developers, add users, then decide to rename to devs; run groupmod -n devs developers, then verify /etc/group and file ownership. Remember three practical concepts as you apply these skills. First: numeric IDs matter — the kernel uses UIDs and GIDs, so always check numeric IDs when behavior is unexpected. Second: use the right flags — usermod -aG appends supplementary groups; omitting -a replaces them and can remove access accidentally. Third: verify after changes — id, grep in /etc/passwd and /etc/group, and use df -h and free -h to capture a system snapshot. These checks keep your systems auditable and reduce accidental lockouts or permission mistakes.
